summary: Academic empirical study of how the agent harness (not the model) affects SE-agent results. It compares mini-SWE-agent vs OpenCode with ten Qwen/DeepSeek open-weight models on SWE-bench Pro, ProgramBench and GitTaskBench, then builds NanoHarness (mini-SWE-agent plus switchable tool registry, context compression, todo planning, general/task-specific subagents, lazy SKILL.md skills) and ablates each component on ProgramBench with two models.

claims.claim: Marginal benefit of a complex harness shrinks as model capability rises on SWE-style issue repair.
claims.evidence: Table 3 (SWE-bench Verified leaderboard, not the authors' runs): OpenHands gain +13.60 -> +5.47 pp, SWE-agent +9.60 -> +4.07 pp from Claude 3.7 to Claude 4 Sonnet. Own runs on 300-instance SWE-bench Pro sample: Qwen OpenCode advantage ~6 pp -> 2.67 pp (Fig. 5); DeepSeek non-monotonic, V4-Pro 34.3 vs 33.7 (Fig. 6). Single run per cell, no CIs; DeepSeek pattern only partly fits the claim.

claims.claim: On newer open-ended repository tasks (ProgramBench, GitTaskBench) complex harnesses help stronger models more (capability amplifier).
claims.evidence: Figs 7-10 only (no numeric tables in text); N=70 ProgramBench sample and N=54 GitTaskBench, single run each; turning points stated qualitatively.

claims.claim: Tool registry and task-specific subagents give the most stable component gains; context compression and general subagents hurt.
claims.evidence: §5.2.1 text: tools +4.57 / +3.54 pp, task-specific subagents +5.91 / +4.46 pp, context compression -4.86 / -3.85 pp (Qwen3.7-Max / DeepSeek-V4-Pro) on full 200-task ProgramBench. Two models, one run each, no variance; compression is one particular LLM-summarize-at-350K implementation; task-specific subagents (behavior analysis, differential testing, submission review) were designed for ProgramBench's reference-binary setting.

claims.claim: Full NanoHarness improves over mini-SWE-agent by 7.37 and 6.21 pp and recovers most of the gap to product harnesses.
claims.evidence: Table 6: 42.88 -> 50.25 (Qwen3.7-Max), 45.14 -> 51.35 (DeepSeek-V4-Pro); OpenCode 51.68/52.48, Claude Code 52.33/52.76. Numbers match the abstract (Table 6 mislabels pp gains as '%'). No variance, so 1-2 pp gaps to product harnesses are within plausible run-to-run noise; designed and evaluated on the same benchmark.

claims.claim: Gains come from structured interaction, not more prompt budget.
claims.evidence: Table 7: NanoHarness tool calls +131.18% / +83.58% but prompt tokens +16.37% / +7.26%; context compression cuts prompt tokens 54.29% / 77.02% while scores drop. Supported as a token accounting; causal 'regularized exploration' story rests on Fig. 13 distribution plus two hand-picked cases (jq, calcurse).

patterns.note: LLM-summarization context compression (350K budget, keep last 20 messages) reduced ProgramBench score by 4.86 / 3.85 pp despite 54-77% prompt-token savings.
Task-specific subagents with restricted tool whitelists and fresh history: largest single gain (+5.91 / +4.46 pp); generic SDLC-role subagents hurt.
Generic role-based subagents (requirement_analysis, architecture_design, code_generation, test_generation, defect_repair) degraded performance for both models.
Lazy-loaded SKILL.md catalog with load_skill(): small/model-dependent gains, larger for DeepSeek-V4-Pro than Qwen3.7-Max.
TodoWrite-style planning gave small gains only, at +21% prompt tokens for Qwen.
Bash-only mini-SWE-agent loop was beaten by adding structured native tools (read/write/edit/glob) by 3.5-4.6 pp on ProgramBench, i.e. pure shell-as-action was not optimal here.
Minimal single-loop harness is within 0.6-2.7 pp of OpenCode on SWE-bench Pro for the strongest models, but trails by 7-9 pp on ProgramBench.
All evidence is benchmark-based (SWE-bench Pro, ProgramBench, GitTaskBench) plus leaderboard-scraped SWE-bench Verified numbers.
Reports per-config token usage and total cost (> $7,000; >10B/20B prompt tokens); step caps reduced to 300 on ProgramBench.
Docker with --network none, resource limits, SYS_PTRACE disabled for evaluation.

[retag 2026-10-07] No fixed workflow is evaluated. The SDLC-ordered general subagents (requirement_analysis ... defect_repair) are invoked on demand by the parent loop (§3), so their ProgramBench loss for both models (§5.2.1) is not evidence about a fixed lifecycle pipeline. Agentless-style localization-repair-validation pipelines appear only in related work (§6.2), and §5.1.2 calls SWE-bench Pro's task workflow 'relatively fixed'.

methodology.sample: RQ1: 300-instance random sample of SWE-bench Pro (731), 70 of 200 ProgramBench, all 54 GitTaskBench; RQ2/3: full 200 ProgramBench, 2 models x 8 configs.
methodology.baselines: mini-SWE-agent (minimal) and OpenCode (product-level); Claude Code added only in Table 6. Baselines are current, untuned by authors.
methodology.models: 10 open-weight models (5 Qwen: Qwen3-Max..Qwen3.7-Max; 5 DeepSeek: R1..V4-Pro), non-thinking mode; no closed models in own runs.
methodology.variance: Temperature 0, apparently one run per configuration; no seeds, CIs or significance tests.
methodology.ablations: Single-component add-ons and all-on; no leave-one-out from the full configuration, so interactions are not isolated.
methodology.contamination_controls: None; authors themselves suggest SWE-style task-specific training may explain smaller harness dependence on SWE-bench Pro (§5.1.2).
methodology.languages: SWE-bench Pro: Python, JS/TS, Go; ProgramBench: Rust, Go, C/C++, Java, Haskell; GitTaskBench: Python. No per-language breakdown.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint; no venue in comment or journal_ref.
standards.artifacts: No code or data link for NanoHarness, prompts, or trajectories found in the text; only OpenCode's repo cited.

biases.detail: Single temperature-0 run per cell; 1-2 pp gaps (NanoHarness vs OpenCode/Claude Code) and several component deltas are reported without any uncertainty.

Task-specific subagents (behavior analysis, differential testing vs reference binary) and skills like CLI Fuzzing are tailored to ProgramBench, then evaluated on ProgramBench with no held-out benchmark for the component study.
NanoHarness is the authors' own harness, built and scored by the authors on the same benchmark used to design it.
RQ1.1 harness-vs-capability trend partly relies on SWE-bench Verified leaderboard numbers (Table 3) from heterogeneous third-party submissions, not controlled runs.
Failure-mode analysis illustrated with two selected instances (jqlang__jq, lfos__calcurse).
No release of NanoHarness code, prompts, or trajectories despite claiming a reusable modular harness.
Only Qwen and DeepSeek families in own runs; frontier closed models (Claude/GPT) appear only via leaderboard numbers.

verdict_reason: Headline numbers (7.37/6.21 pp, component deltas) are present in Table 6 and §5.2, and the 10-model x 3-benchmark matrix with two harnesses is broader than most harness papers. But every cell is a single run without variance, the component study is designed and tested on one benchmark (ProgramBench), and no NanoHarness artifact is released, so treat component rankings as directional.
applicability: Directly informs harness decisions. For a Java backend team: (1) give agents structured read/edit/glob tools rather than raw bash only; (2) prefer narrowly scoped, task-specific subagents (e.g. an contract checker, a differential tester, a pre-submission reviewer) over generic 'architect/coder/tester' role agents, which hurt here; (3) be cautious with automatic LLM summarization compaction on long multi-repo work tasks where specs and interface constraints must survive the whole run—keep the spec in a re-readable file instead; (4) lazy skills are cheap but give modest gains. Caveats: Java is only one of five ProgramBench languages with no per-language breakdown, nothing is cross-repository (several repositories), and the 'model capability shrinks harness gains' finding means harness tuning done for one agent host/model in a mixed-host shop may not transfer. Spec-driven development is not tested, though the compression result supports keeping specs as persistent artifacts outside conversational context.

conflicts_with.detail: AttnCompress argues trajectory compression can preserve SE-task evidence while cutting context; here generic compression cut tokens 54-77% but reduced ProgramBench scores by ~4-5 pp.
FOCUS claims decision-preserving compression helps agents; this paper finds compression hurts on long repository-generation tasks (different compression method).

Scaffold Effect finds within-model pass-rate differences across harnesses of 0-8 pp with paired bootstrap CIs mostly including zero, versus this paper's uncertainty-free claims of meaningful 1-9 pp harness/component effects.
